text: A realm above you can kill you as a grown man kills a child, and nobody asks why. Juniors call any higher realm 'senior', bow first and speak second; peers are 'fellow daoist'. Offend a senior and only someone stronger standing behind you keeps you alive.

Immortals are not argued with. You bow low or kneel, call them 'immortal master', answer what they ask and never ask back. An immortal who kills a mortal answers to nobody but his own sect, and sects seldom ask.

Mortals are beneath a cultivator's notice unless they're in the way. Most cultivators are not cruel to them, only careless; killing one in a city still brings the watch, and killing one in a sect's county brings the sect.

Sweeping a stranger with divine sense to read their cultivation is rude, and a senior who notices may take it as a slight. A realm you can't see through is a warning: they may be far above you, so you are polite until you know.

In a sect, whoever entered before you is senior brother or senior sister whatever their age, and whoever came after is junior. An elder is Elder and a surname; your own master is Master, and his other disciples your martial brothers and sisters.

A cultivator with a craft is worth more than one without: everyone needs an alchemist's pills, a refiner's blades and an array master's wards. Even sect elders speak softly to a good alchemist, and a grade from a guild hall opens doors a realm doesn't.

Heaven narrows at every gate. Of thirty at Qi Condensation, one reaches Foundation; of sixty at Foundation, one forms a core. Most cultivators grow old at the ninth layer waiting for a Foundation Pill they never get.
Methods are kept in jade slips, read by pressing one to the brow. A power's own method is guarded: copying it, selling it, or throwing its arts where its people can see brings its law hall after you.
Immortals eat pills the way rich men eat ginseng. The one they fight over is said to make them truly immortal; a whole town's silver wouldn't buy one, and no mortal you know has ever held one.
Immortals live for centuries; the old ones in the sects watched your great-grandfather born. A mortal gets sixty years if the harvests are kind and the beasts stay south.
Silver taels are honest money. Immortals pay in spirit stones, faintly glowing and worth more than a field; a mortal who finds one sells it fast to a money-changer and tells nobody.

On testing day the immortals touch every child's hand to a stone, and one in a few thousand lights it. That child is taken away to cultivate and the family is paid for it; the rest go back to the fields.

Sixty-six thousand years ago the Heaven Ladder to the great world above broke, out in the Shattered Sea. Since then nobody here ascends: the greatest cultivators grow old under a closed sky. Every child knows the story, and every old cultivator half believes it.
Years are counted in the Sealed Era, now in its fourth thousand years. Older eras are names in sect libraries and nothing more to most people.

Outside a city's walls or a sect's grounds, what happens between cultivators is their own business. Kill a man where nobody sees and the only trouble is his backers: a soul lamp goes out in his sect, and they come asking.

Nobody on the frontier stands alone if they can help it. Before you strike a cultivator you ask who stands behind him: a sect, a clan, a master a realm above. Young masters say their father's name early for that reason.
